newsitem.title: PERU: Fujimori tells Peru rebels no one backs them.
newsitem.headline: Fujimori tells Peru rebels no one backs them.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori, leaving Lima on Tuesday for the first time since Peru's four-week hostage crisis began, visited the site of one of his victories against leftist rebels.
He used the visit to proclaim that no one in country supported the Marxist hostage-takers.

The International Committee of the Red Cross said it would accept an invitation to join a "guarantor commission" to try to end the standoff peacefully, and the Vatican envoy to the government-proposed commission said he believed talks between the government and the rebels would begin soon.

Fujimori took Ecuador's President Abdala Bucaram, who is in Peru on an official visit, to the Andean mountain province of Ayacucho and showed him the village of Vilcashuaman, a former centre of guerrilla activity that has been placed back under government control.

"All Peruvians have clearly demonstrated that the people reject violence," Fujimori told a cheering crowd against the dramatic Andean backdrop. "All of Peru is against this hostage-taking and demands their freedom."
Maoist Shining Path guerrillas began their revolution in Ayacucho and controlled large areas throughout the 1980s, but were ousted by government forces in the early 1990s.

Fujimori says he has broken the back of Shining Path and the once less-known Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movemement (MRTA), and that the MRTA hostage-takers, who are holding 74 people at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima, are acting out of desperation.

Roman Catholic Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani, a close friend of Fujimori named by the Vatican to sit on the proposed guarantor commission, travelled with Fujimori and called on all sides to sit down for talks as soon as possible.

"My constant request is that God move everyone as soon as possible to start a dialogue which surely will bring peace," Cipriani said. "Please, trusting in God, trusting in truth and openness, sit down to talk. We wish for this, and I believe it will soon happen."
Red Cross spokeswoman Cecilia Baux told Reuters the organisation would join the commission if and when it is formally set up.
"We can participate in the commission but only in matters of a humanitarian nature," she said.
Earlier on Tuesday, a suspected sniper fired three shots outside the besieged Japanese ambassador's home, rattling nerves and increasing tension at the site.

The bullets whizzed over the heads of reporters on the roof of a neighbouring house overlooking the diplomatic residence and disappeared into the darkness. It was not clear who fired the shots, which unlike previous instances of gunfire at the site, seemed to come from outside the compound.
"Each one sounded like a low thud as if they came from a silenced gun. They passed over so close I could hear them sizzling," said Gregg Newton, a Reuters photographer.
"We do not know where they came from," Baux said. "The situation is totally calm."
There were no reports of injuries.

The approximately 15 rebels, who stormed a reception at the residence on Dec. 17 and took hundreds of guests hostage, are armed with rifles and grenades and have booby-trapped and mined the compound against a surprise attack.
Fujimori has said he will not use force to end the siege unless the hostages are harmed.

The rebels, who have released the majority of the original 500 hostages, have asked for a local television crew to be let into the residence to broadcast their answer to the government's guarantor commission proposal.
But government negotiator, Education Minister Domingo Palermo, told reporters he believed the television station did not want to be "a channel of communication for the MRTA."

The negotiations have bogged down in uncompromising positions. The guerrillas have refused to back down on their demand that some 400 jailed MRTA comrades be freed. The government has flatly rejected the demand.
